Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review
Anurag Chakraborti<sup>1</sup> Suman Kalyan Das<sup>1</sup> Prasanta Sahoo<sup>1</sup>
Received: 3 March 2025 / Accepted: 13 August 2025
© King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals 2025
Abstract
This comprehensive review explores electroless cobalt deposition, an appealing surface modification technique that offers
advantages such as uniform coverage on complex geometries and compatibility with diverse substrate materials without
external power. The article systematically examines the critical impact of various bath constituents and operational variables
on the characteristics of deposited films. It details the roles of the cobalt source, different reducing agents, complexing agents,
pH regulators, and stabilizers. Additionally, the article scrutinizes the influence of deposition parameters like temperature,
solution pH, agitation methods, and bath aging. The formation of numerous cobalt-based alloys and composite materials are
also discussed. This review aims to guide the development of optimized electroless cobalt plating solutions, highlighting their
wide-ranging utility in fields such as microelectronics, data storage, protective coatings, electrolytic green H₂ generation
metal matrix composites, and electromagnetic shielding, thereby fostering advancements in intricate material fabrication

any surface. Unlike traditional electroplating, which relies
on external electrical current, electroless cobalt utilizes a
chemical reduction process. This eliminates the need for
exclusively conducting substrates, complex electrical setup
and allows for more uniform deposition on intricate surfaces.
The process is steadily gaining traction since its inception by
Brenner and Riddell [1] in 1947 due to simplicity of the tech-
nique and lower cost of instrumentation. Electroless coating
or autocatalytic coating is a category of chemical process that
deposits one or more metal layers by autocatalytic reduction
of metal cations in a liquid chemical bath. One of the signifi-
cant advantages of electroless plating is its ability to achieve
a more even and conformal coating compared to electroplat-
ing. Unlike electroplating, homogeneity of deposit thickness
is maintained even in the sharp corners or intricate recesses of
the substrate surface [2, 3]. This characteristic makes it ideal
for applications where uniform coverage is crucial, such as in
microelectronics and the fabrication of magnetic thin films.
The composition of the electroless plating solution can be tai-
lored to control the properties of the deposited cobalt layer.
Electroless cobalt alloy finds applications in various fields.
In the microelectronics industry, it is used to create diffusion
barriers [4, 5] and seed layers [6, 7] for subsequent electro-
plating processes. The magnetic properties ofcobalt make it a
valuable material for data storage devices and magnetic sen-
sors [8, 9]. Since US Environmental Protection Agency (US
EPA) categorized Cr<sup>6+</sup> containing baths (essential for hard
chrome plating) as unsuitable for environment and stressed
on alternative approaches [10], cobalt-based plating has also
been explored and employed for wear [11–13] and corrosion
[14, 15] protection of metallic components. While electro-
less plating excels at creating thin films, its potential extends
far beyond simple flat surfaces. Deposition of 3D struc-
tures like cobalt microspheres [16, 17] and 1D structures
like nanowires [18] or nanotubes [19] has been successfully
demonstrated, paving the way for a new generation of micro
and nanostructured materials with enhanced functionalities
in various fields.

is scarce. Shen et al. [20] in 2022 provided a summary
on the progress of electroless cobalt deposition narrowly
focusing on semiconductor-based electronics application.

marize past works on the influence of bath composition and
coating parameters on autocatalytic cobalt deposition. The
article also includes brief discussion on the development of
Co-based alloys and composites structures obtained via elec-
troless path and their intended applications.
2 Electroless Cobalt Deposition Process
The deposition process involves reduction ofcobalt cations in
an aqueous solution ofmetal salt in the presence ofa reducing
agent (R) at the surface of a catalytic substrate. Deposition
then continues due to the catalytic action of the deposited
metal ions. Hence, the process is also named as autocatalytic.
In the course of time, four different detailed reaction mech-
anisms were proposed to account for electroless deposition
process [21]. Among them, the electrochemical mechanism
has been experimentally validated by Hwang et al. [22]
specifically in case of cobalt deposition. According to this
proposition catalyst particles jump start the oxidation (loss
of electrons) of reducing agent by acting as anode whereas
reduction (gain of electrons) of metal cations happens at a
different cathodic site with less catalytic activity. General
chemical reaction for the electroless metal deposition pro-
cess can be expressed as:
\text { Anodic   Reaction }: \mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{R} ^ {\mathrm{z} +} + \mathrm{ze} ^ {-}\tag{1}

The aqueous bath primarily consists of a cobalt salt as the
source of cobalt ions, a reducing agent to convert cobalt
cations to cobalt atoms, complexing agent, pH regulator, and
stabilizer. The prepared solution is heated and maintained at
certain temperature, and activated substrate is immersed in
the heated solution for deposition. Deposition process can

The specific constituents, including the cobalt salt, reduc-
ing agent, complexing agent, stabilizer, are paramount in
dictating the deposition characteristics. Understanding these
individual components is therefore essential for optimizing
the electroless cobalt deposition.

Use of sodium hypophosphite causes incorporation of P
in the cobalt matrix. Miksic et al. [40] provided the earliest
report on the amount of P present in Co matrix deposited
with different hypophosphite concentration. They found that
increasing hypophosphite concentration from 0.047 M to
0.24 M resulted in an increase of the P content from 0.5% to
2.5%. Frieze et al. [41] varied the hypophosphite concentra-
tion within slightly wider range (0.05 M to 0.5 M). They were
able to increase the amount of P from 1% to 5%. Schlesinger
et al. [42] obtained Co-P deposits with the amount of P rang-
ing from 3% to 12% and found almost linear relationship
between P content and hypophosphite concentration. They
also conclusively observed the tendency of decreasing grain
size with increasing amount ofP which was previously hinted
by the observations of Cortijo et al. [43]. During nucleation
and subsequent growth of Co film on the substrate surface,
P atoms act as growth inhibitor resulting in smaller grain
size [41, 44]. Dark field transmission electron micrograph
[45] and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy [46] along
the grain boundaries suggest that P atoms accumulate along
the grain boundaries preventing further grain growth.
Among boron containing reducing agents, Pearlstein et al.
[47] initially investigated the role of DMAB as reducing
agent and observed linear increase of deposition rate with
increasing DMAB concentration up to 0.07 M. They were
able to incorporate maximum of 1.7% B in the Co matrix
resulting in a bright and smooth deposit. Addition of further
DMAB caused rapid bath decomposition. Saito et al. [48] and
Rohan et al. [49] also independently observed linear relation-
ship between deposition rate and concentration of DMAB in
the bath. Additionally, Saito et al. [48] reported that amount
of B reaches at its peak at 0.075 M DMAB concentration. It is
noteworthy that DMAB loses electrons more readily than Co
at the vicinity of Cu substrate. Because of this Co can directly
be reduced on the otherwise non-catalytic Cu surface with-
out any pre-activation [50]. Morpholine borane (MB) acts in
a similar manner as DMAB [51]. The generalized reaction
can be expressed as:

\begin{array}{r l}&\mathrm {R.NHBH_ {3}} + 4 \mathrm {H_ {2} O} + 1. 5 \mathrm {Co^ {2 + }}\\&\rightarrow 1. 5 \mathrm{Co} + \mathrm {R.NH^ {+}} + \mathrm{B(OH)} ^ {4 -} + 2 \mathrm {H_ {2}} + 6 \mathrm {H^ {+}}\end{array}\tag{4}
Here, R is an organic group. Increase in deposition rate
with MB concentration is significant up to a value of 0.05 M;
further increase has a diminishing effect on the deposi-
tion rate. Sodium borohydride has also been successfully
employed by Dai et al. [52, 53] to reduce electroless cobalt
bath although its role as reducing agent was not the focus
of the reports. It can be assumed that role of borohydride in
reduction of cobalt is somewhat similar to nickel reduction.
Reduction using hydrazine
produces deposition
of pure cobalt (> 99.85%) powder [35, 54] or thin film [55].
The relation between rate of deposition and hydrazine con-
centration is almost linear. The reduction mechanism can be
expressed as [54]-
\mathrm{N} _ {2} \mathrm{H} _ {4} + 4 \mathrm{OH} ^ {-} \rightarrow \mathrm{N} _ {2} + 4 \mathrm{H} _ {2} \mathrm{O} + 4 \mathrm{e} ^ {-}\tag{5}
\mathrm{Co} ^ {2 +} + 2 \mathrm{e} ^ {-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Co}\tag{6}
2 \mathrm{H} _ {2} \mathrm{O} + 2 \mathrm{e} ^ {-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H} _ {2} + 2 \mathrm{OH} ^ {-}\tag{7}

content in the deposit typically increases with higher con-
centrations of hypophosphite (Fig. 3a) and DMAB (Fig. 3b),
respectively. Concurrently, Fig. 3c shows that the deposition
rate generally rises with increasing reductant concentration.

In electroless plating, both ultrasonication and stirring serve
the same overall purpose, which is to ensure a uniform and
high-quality metal deposition on the surface of the object
being plated. Ultrasonication uses high-frequency sound
waves to create microscopic vibrations in the solution to
dislodge gas bubbles and enhance mass transfer [82]. In

reaction requires less energy to occur, allowing for a com-

found that at high ultrasonication power (100 W), the film
exhibits cracks on the surface. This is likely because exces-
sive agitation disrupts the film growth process, leading to
weak bonding between the deposited particles and creating
cracks. They recommend 90 W for deposition of relatively
smaller and more regular shaped crystallites.

7 Electroless Co composites
Co composites formed from electroless bath can be of two
types – Co matrix composite and core shell composite.
Evenly dispersing inorganic foreign particles like WS [115],
SiC [116], or BN [70] in the electroless Co bath with the help
of a surfactant (CTAB or SLS) and then depositing Co from
this bath on an activated surface yield Co-WS , Co-SiC, or
Co-BN composite films, respectively. In this type of compos-
ites, these nano or micron-sized inorganic particles are evenly
distributed in the Co film to form metal matrix composites.
In case of core shell composites, ceramic particle cores
or any fiber can be coated with Co to form the composites.
The process scheme is shown in Fig. 8c, and SEM image
of a core shell composite is shown in Fig. 8c’. Micron-sized
WC particles [117, 118], MgO nanoparticles [119], zirconia
alumina (ZTA) composite macroparticles [120], or micron-
sized hydroxyapatite (HA) particles [121] were activated and
immersed in the Co bath to coat each particle with cobalt
to, respectively, form Co-WC, Co-MgO, Co-ZTA, or Co-
HA core shell composite microspheres. A fibrous material
like glass fibers [75, 122], SiC whiskers [123], or multiwall
carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) [124] can also be activated and
placed in the electroless bath to coat each fiber with cobalt
in a similar manner to form core shell composite fibers.
8 Applications
Electroless cobalt, a versatile thin film deposited through a
chemical process, boasts a distinct set of properties that have
driven its adoption in various established industries. How-
ever, recent research is also exploring its potential in exciting
new frontiers. Major areas of applications are schematically
represented in Fig. 9.
8.1 Traditional Applications
8.1.1 Magnetic Recording
Magnetic properties ofelectroless Co films, particularly coer-
civity, have been extensively studied from the beginning.
Coercivity is the ability of a ferromagnetic material to resist
external magnetic field without being magnetized. Tune-
able coercivity of electroless Co-P combined with ultra-thin
nature of the deposited film makes it a candidate of inter-
est for high density magnetic recording medium [8, 9, 78].
Ouchi et al. [125] fabricated CoNiP nanodot arrays shorter
than 50 nm with high perpendicular magnetic coercivities,
using electroless deposition process (Fig. 10a). This is a
crucial property for perpendicular magnetic recording tech-
nology to increase storage density. Co-P films are promising
for magnetic rotary encoders, enabling magnetization into
2048 magnetic pole pairs with uniform output [126]. This
improves resolution and accuracy for angle and displacement
measurements.
8.1.2 Tribological Applications
Electroless Co-P deposits typically have a fine-grained struc-
ture, which contributes to their low friction coefficients and
good wear resistance. However, the wear and friction behav-
ior of the deposit can be further improved by annealing the
deposit at an elevated temperature. Annealing causes the
metal grains to grow, which results in a more uniform and
stronger deposit. Klingenberg et al. [127]reported the micro-
hardness (VHN) of Co-B to be 716 kg-f/mm<sup>2</sup> and of Co-P
to be 883 kg-f/mm<sup>2</sup> after heat treatment at 350 °C. Com-
posite coating like Co-SiC can exhibit high hardness even
without heat treatment [116]. Self-lubricating Co-WS film
(Fig. 10b) with very low coefficient of friction can be pro-
duced via electroless route [115]. It is also reported that

10 Conclusions
Electroless cobalt plating is a versatile technique capable of
depositing a wide range of cobalt-based coatings, including
pure cobalt and various binary and ternary alloys such as
Co-P, Co-B, Co–Ni-P, Co-W–P, and Co-W-B. By carefully
adjusting the composition of the plating bath and oper-
ating conditions, it is possible to tailor the properties of
the deposited coatings to meet specific application require-
ments. These coatings offer numerous advantages, including
improved corrosion and wear resistance, enhanced magnetic
information storage capabilities, ability to serve as effec-
tive barrier layers against copper diffusion or acting as a
catalyst in H generation via electrolysis. While many poten-
tial applications have been explored, there is still significant
room for further research and development in this area. This
review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of
the electroless cobalt plating process by serving as a valu-
able resource for information on the various chemical baths
and operating conditions employed by previous researchers.
